title.analysis: Exact title: What Net Worth Makes You Rich, Middle, or Poor? (47 characters). A direct question with three contrasting status categories offers personal placement and an apparently objective threshold answer. Title case; no numerical threshold, all-caps threat or deadline. Net worth is a precise search keyword, while rich/middle/poor supplies broad social-comparison appeal. US geography is absent from packaging but explicit in narration. Search ranking/volume unknown.

script.analysis: All 19377 stored characters read in six contiguous 3500-character chunks; source hash verified, audio not reviewed. Opening uses social-media Europe/Tesla comparison and anxious account checking, then promises shocking exact class boundaries. Creator introduction and subscribe/like precede first numerical payoff. Median-versus-mean contrast establishes inequality, followed by lower → lower-middle → middle → upper-middle/HENRY → upper → top 1%/0.1% ladder. Repeated teasers about the next class sustain a staircase open loop; examples of debt, emergencies, professions and lifestyle inflation translate labels into everyday implications. Geographic caveat comes late and switches from net worth to state earnings. Final shift toward looking wealthy versus being wealthy uses Buffett anecdote and opportunity cost, then closes with snapshot-not-life-sentence encouragement and next-video CTA. No clean definition/formula for net worth despite exact classification promise; no reproducible table or primary citation detail in narration. Social-class threshold gaps, inconsistent medians and mixed denominators compromise educational payoff. Some lower-resource constraints are acknowledged, unlike the previous psychology-only savings video; later anyone-can-climb framing still overstates agency. Retention effects of preamble/teasers unknown. ASR numerical fragments and malformed words preserved; no silent repair.

claim_audit: Fed 2022 SCF corroborates median family net worth $192900, mean $1063700 (about $1.06m), and 37% inflation-adjusted median growth from 2019. Script supplies year but calls units household; SCF family definition matters, not individual universal benchmark. Wealth mean/median ratio about5.51 is mathematically possible; height analogy illustrates skew, not a statistical equivalence. Stored 8t may be ASR, do not repair.

Top1% almost32% total wealth is plausible context but no quarter, series or source specified. Fed DFA is a dated distributional series, not an official lower/middle/upper social-class taxonomy. One in100 is top1%; later three people at100-person party analogy is internally inconsistent. Household net wealth also does not mean one-third of everything valuable in the country, which includes assets outside that accounting universe.

Lower-class $0–16900 and median just over6000 attributed to Fed without percentile or methodology. Negative-net-worth households fall outside stated lower bound; student-loan caveat acknowledges negatives but does not fix coverage. Official Census poverty is based on family money-income thresholds varying by composition, not these net-worth limits. Technical poverty-class claim unsupported.

Lower-middle stored range is $16900 to $43000 followed by separate $1760 fragment, then median $61260. Median exceeds stated upper bound. Could reflect damaged ASR, but canonical text cannot support a clean repaired threshold. Middle $58550–169420 with median145200 has unexplained gap from lower-middle; upper-middle500000–2m leaves169420–500000 unclassified, and upper2.65m leaves2m–2.65m unclassified. Ranges do not form complete exclusive ladder; no source establishes official class cutoffs.

Top1% asserted at5.8m, then acknowledged10m/12m; top0.1%62m unsupported source/date/population. Individual versus household, adult/global versus US, survey weights, inflation date and assets included can change cutoffs; billionaires price fluctuations alone insufficient explanation. Do not select one as verified household threshold. Upperclass2.65m likewise unverified; HENRY earnings140k not universal definition or proof of500k–2m assets.

Connecticut top1% income over1m and WestVirginia416k lack year/tax-unit/source. Income thresholds are flows, not net-worth stock thresholds and do not validate geographic wealth class. Cost of living can alter consumption utility, not national percentile at a fixed valuation.2m cannot literally buy anything wanted even in cheaper town. Local opportunity/career/tax/moving costs omitted.

Profession, homeownership, ability to max retirement, credit access and benefit eligibility cannot be inferred solely from net worth. Program eligibility and income taxes vary by income/assets/household/program, not broad label. High earners may receive SocialSecurity despite lower replacement rates; expected fund own retirement entirely too sweeping.

Buffett house1958/31500 and current650k value/100bn fortune not independently verified here; time-sensitive appraisal/wealth and one anecdote not population evidence. Known modest consumption does not establish private spending thought processes or all wealth origins. Wealth did not get there by accident ignores acknowledged inheritance/luck. Opportunity cost principle useful, contingent returns not guaranteed; no quantitative forecast made.

topic.analysis: US wealth distribution, net-worth benchmarking, class identity, inequality and geographic purchasing power. Evergreen self-placement problem with dated SCF inputs and fast-changing upper-tail claims. Beginner accessible but mixes descriptive distribution and normative status labels. Primary statistics give partial grounding, not validation of full ladder. No reliable publication-linked demand or historical Trends evidence.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: Three-way class question versus age benchmarks and life-changing threshold titles. Distinct audience promise is placement, not a personalized plan; threshold accuracy is central.
topic.competition: Same-channel benchmark and milestone titles range weak to strong; broader saturation and actual recommendation competition unavailable.
